column1: # ================ *** KATHLEEN GEORGINA TAYLOR: THE ANSWER *** ================
# This archive asked whether the eldest of the ten ever married. The 1911 census found her SINGLE at
# forty-one in her sister's house. The 1921 census finds her *** STILL THERE AT FIFTY *** - and gives
# the reason, in the occupation column:
#                        *** "HOME INVALID" ***
# *** That is not a date or a surname. It is a life. *** The eldest daughter of ten, unmarried at fifty,
# an invalid in her younger sister's house on Fore Street, with her brother-in-law the insurance agent
# and three children about her. She died in 1940, aged sixty-nine. Nothing in this archive had suggested
# it, because a tree records marriages and not infirmity.
# *** AND THE INDEX CALLS HER "KATHLEEN GEORGINA DALLING". *** She is a TAYLOR. The enumerator wrote the
# household's surname against every line and the transcriber followed him. *** THIS IS THE EXACT TRAP
# THAT COST THIS ARCHIVE A RETRACTION IN ARGENTINA *** - the 1895 Buenos Aires census, where "Lerena de
# L. Josefa" was read as a woman who married a Lerena and turned out to be household shorthand. The same
# enumerator's habit, in Devon, twenty-six years later, in English.
# ================ *** A BIRTHPLACE THAT IS SIMPLY WRONG, AND WHY *** ================
# The 1921 return gives IRENE's birthplace as *** BERMONDSEY, LONDON ***. She was born at NORTHAM in
# 1879 - her own marriage act of 30 August 1900 says so, and the 1911 census says so. Her husband HENRY
# ALBERT BURTON was genuinely born at Bermondsey. *** He filled the form - the transcript names "person
# making return" - and carried his own answer across to his wife's line. ***
# Recorded because it is a worked example of something this archive keeps meeting: *** a census
# birthplace is only as good as the person who filled the form, *** and one household member's answer
# can contaminate another's. Had Irene been met first in 1921, she would have been ruled out as a
# Londoner.
